claims.text: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi is a high-entropy alloy whose mechanical behavior depends on temperature.
The deformation mechanism shifts from dislocation nucleation and phase reorientation at low temperature to dislocation multiplication and twinning at elevated temperature.
The as-prepared equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi alloy has a single-phase FCC structure.
Mechanical testing from approximately 77 K to 800 °C spans temperature regimes relevant to the alloy's temperature-dependent behavior.
Dislocation networks, twin boundaries, and crystallographic reorientation regions evolve with temperature in CoCrFeMnNi.
At low temperature, high surface energy favors partial-dislocation nucleation and phase reorientation in CoCrFeMnNi.
Lattice distortion favors the low-temperature nucleation and propagation of partial dislocations in CoCrFeMnNi.
Low-temperature partial-dislocation activity and phase reorientation produce superplastic-like behavior in CoCrFeMnNi.
At elevated temperature, thermal activation increases dislocation mobility and suppresses complete phase reorientation.
At elevated temperature, increased dislocation multiplication and twinning sustain plastic flow and balance work hardening with ductility.
Low-temperature deformation gives higher yield strength and enhanced work hardening.
Low-temperature deformation produces evidence of phase reorientation and twinning in CoCrFeMnNi.
Elevated-temperature deformation gives lower yield strength while maintaining ductility through thermally activated dislocation processes.
SLM-built equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi retains comparatively high strength up to approximately 700–800 °C.
At room temperature, CoCrFeMnNi exhibits a balance of strength and ductility.
Room-temperature properties of SLM-built CoCrFeMnNi are influenced by fine grains, dislocation networks, and nanoscale oxides.
Far beyond 800 °C or below the examined cryogenic range, phase stability may be compromised and the proposed deformation mechanisms may cease to dominate.
The quantitative changes in yield strength, ductility, and the relative contributions of dislocation activity and twinning remain experimentally uncertain.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and mechanism characterize twinning as part of the elevated-temperature mechanism, whereas the predicted outcome also assigns twinning to the low-temperature regime, obscuring the claimed mechanism switch.
